remarks: The source document does not provide quantified percentages for delays, duplicate documents, consultant dependency or cost burden; such figures should not be inferred.

findings.text: The CTE application process is fully online through the State single-window system, and the applicant is not required to physically visit the State Pollution Control Board for submission.
The prescribed/indicative processing timeline discussed for CTE is approximately 60 days.
Where Environmental Clearance is applicable, the applicant must separately use the PARIVESH portal for the EC-related requirement, adding an inter-portal step.
Site inspection remains a mandatory physical verification step before CTE is granted, checking site suitability and proposed pollution-control arrangements.

Applicants still need to submit multiple supporting documents, including land documents, Gram Panchayat NOC and company resolution, which can create a burden where applications are incomplete or inappropriate.
Industries are classified as Red, Orange, Green and White based on pollution potential, following CPCB criteria adopted by the State, which determines the level of compliance applicable.
Applications may require additional time beyond the indicative 60 days where documentation is incomplete, clarification is required, or the case is complex/critical.
There is no deemed-approval provision for CTE; the applicant instead has an appeal provision available if the prescribed timeline is exceeded.
The expert suggested improving integration between the State single-window system and the PARIVESH portal.
The expert recommended clearer category-wise guidance for Red, Orange, Green and White industries.
Automated inspection allocation and tracking were identified as practices worth continuing.
Application status can be tracked online, with SMS and email notifications available to applicants.
The expert stated that major bottlenecks previously experienced in the CTE process have largely been removed following Ease of Doing Business reforms.
CPCB is reportedly developing a new central online portal for consent-related processes.
For investment below ₹5 crore, a direct CTO is provided instead of requiring a separate CTE, simplifying the process for smaller investors.
The expert suggested strengthening pre-submission document validation so deficiencies are identified before final submission.

gaps.text: No numerical CTE application fee or category-wise fee schedule is given in the source document.
No validity period or renewal cycle is specified for Consent to Establish.
No average actual processing time is given, only an indicative/prescribed figure of approximately 60 days.
No detailed post-approval compliance checklist (registers, periodic testing, equipment maintenance) is provided beyond general reference to pollution-control compliance.

Fully online CTE submission through the State single-window system eliminates the need for a physical visit to the State Pollution Control Board, with PARIVESH integration for EC cases and SMS/email status tracking.
CPCB is reportedly developing a new central online portal for consent-related processes, which would further digitise the CTE process once operational.

For violations after CTO is granted, the department can issue notices, impose environmental compensation and, where non-compliance continues, order closure.

findings.text: The Factory Licence application process is completely online through the Labour Department portal.
Factory Drawing Approval is required before construction of the factory can commence, as a separate prerequisite step.
Multiple NOCs and supporting documents from different authorities may be required depending on the nature and location of the factory.
Statutory Factory Licence fees increase by 30% every three years; this was identified as a potential area for review.
Incomplete or inappropriate applications are a major source of delay and repeated processing, as applications are returned for correction and resubmission.
Multiple deficiencies or remarks raised across different stages can further extend the effective processing time.
Physical inspection remains mandatory for new Factory Licence applications before the licence is granted.
Random inspection is computer-generated and selected through software as part of the risk-based classification framework.
Inspection observations and show-cause notices are communicated electronically, and compliance/clarification is submitted electronically.
Factory Licence is processed separately after obtaining required approvals such as Factory Drawing Approval, creating scope for repeated documentation across linked services.
The expert recommended expanding risk-based inspections and exempting eligible low-risk factories from mandatory physical inspection where digital verification is sufficient.
The expert recommended operationalising self-certification for eligible factories.
The expert suggested strengthening the online portal with comprehensive document checklists and pre-submission validation.
The expert recommended integrating Factory Building Plan Approval and Factory Licence processes to enable document reuse and minimise repeated documentation.
The expert recommended providing clear guidance and support for investors entering Chhattisgarh from other states regarding applicable Factory Licence requirements and compliance procedures.
Applications and their status can be tracked online.

gaps.text: No numerical statutory or average processing timeline for Factory Licence is stated in this ED.
No validity period or renewal cycle for Factory Licence is stated in this ED.
No base/numeric fee figures are given, only fee determinants (installed power, manpower, construction cost) and the 30% triennial increase.

The 30% statutory fee increase every three years was flagged by the expert as a potential area for review.
Integration of Factory Building Plan Approval and Factory Licence processes was recommended to reduce repeated documentation across linked services.
Computer-generated random selection for inspection reduces discretion in choosing which factories receive physical inspection.

findings.text: The entire land allotment process is digitised through an online portal integrated with the Chhattisgarh e-Procurement system, with applicants using Digital Signature Certificates to register and participate.
Vacant plots, plot size, base price and other plot details, as well as application status, are displayed online, providing transparency.
Applicants pay an initial 10% amount followed by the remaining 90% online before the allotment order is issued.
Stamp duty exemption is available under the State Industrial Policy for eligible industries.
For developed plots, the tender remains open for 21 days before evaluation and allotment.
Multiple internal scrutiny and approval levels increase overall processing time.
Delay in payment of the balance premium by applicants postpones issuance of the allotment order.

Post-allotment processes such as registration, possession certificate and lease execution require coordination with different authorities, including the Registration Department and departmental engineers.

Company incorporation and enterprise-related documents may be required at multiple stages, and registration-related documents are resubmitted again after allotment during lease execution and registration.

Different categories of industries are subject to different land eligibility criteria based on investment size and enterprise category, and industrial areas are classified by the types of industries permitted.
Pollution-intensive industries require additional environmental clearances and approvals before establishment, and additional scrutiny for highly polluting industries can increase processing time.
The recent transition from manual to online land allotment processing is still evolving.
The experts recommended reducing the number of internal approval levels involved in processing land allotment applications.
The experts recommended generating demand notes and allotment orders through a simplified single-click approval mechanism after scrutiny.
The experts recommended simplifying document requirements by seeking only essential documents during the initial application stage.
The experts recommended integrating post-allotment services such as lease transfer, plot merger, mortgage approval and utility services into the online portal.
Land allotment has shifted from first-come-first-served to competitive bidding because of high demand for industrial plots.
Possession certificates are generated online after field verification by departmental engineers.

The 'Documentation Required' section of this document lists items (annual return, compliance information relating to 'the factory', renewal fee via e-Challan) that belong to the Renewal of Factory Licence process rather than Land Allotment, contradicting the rest of the same document, which describes an e-procurement/land-allotment process — likely a copy/drafting error in the source file.
Entire process integrated with the Chhattisgarh e-Procurement portal including DSC-based registration, online plot listing with transparency on price/status, and online payment.
Experts recommended integrating post-allotment services (lease transfer, plot merger, mortgage approval, utility services) into a single online portal and reducing internal approval levels.

findings.text: The Factory Licence renewal process is entirely online, with auto-forwarding and auto-generation of the renewed licence.
The prescribed renewal fee is paid through e-Challan.
Factory Licences can be issued with a validity of up to 15 years, reducing the frequency of conventional renewal requirements.
Annual returns and prescribed compliance information continue to be required even where the licence is subject to auto-renewal.
Delays may arise where prescribed fees, annual returns or required information are not submitted correctly or within the prescribed timeline.
Applicants may require professional or consultant support to complete compliance-related requirements for renewal.
The expert recommended adopting risk-based renewal, avoiding routine physical inspections for low-risk/compliant factories and focusing resources on higher-risk units.
The expert recommended sending automated alerts/reminders before renewal and fee-payment deadlines.
The expert recommended introducing automated pre-validation of annual return information before submission.
The expert recommended retaining a simplified single-click renewal workflow requiring only prescribed fee payment and annual information.
Manual departmental intervention is substantially reduced through the automated renewal mechanism.
The broader Factory Licence process has a prescribed timeline of approximately 30 days per this discussion, while the renewal mechanism itself is more automated and has no separately stated time.
No major redundant documentation was specifically identified for renewal; the process has largely been streamlined through online submission, auto-forwarding and auto-generation.
Risk-based renewal can reduce manual intervention for compliant factories while retaining regulatory oversight for higher-risk factories.
Automated reminders and pre-validation were identified as further potential simplifications to the renewal process.
